sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the scope of a military law that removes time limits for prosecuting crimes punishable by death. One side argues this rule applies only to offenses where the death penalty remains a legal option. The other side claims the rule covers all crimes that were historically eligible for capital punishment.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues that Congress intended the unlimited prosecution window to cover all offenses historically eligible for the death penalty.
the opposing side argues that the statute only applies to offenses where the death penalty is currently a legal punishment option.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor asked how the government reconciles its position with the decades-long absence of death penalty sentences in military rape cases.
Justice Thomas asked whether the statute of limitations argument stands independently from the Eighth Amendment question regarding the death penalty's applicability to the military.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether military prosecutors can bring charges for historical rape offenses indefinitely. It defines the scope of time limits for prosecuting serious crimes within the armed forces. The outcome shapes the legal rights of service members facing prosecution for past conduct.
